entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Apollinaris the Elder, a distinguished Christian grammarian active in the 4th century CE, played a pivotal role in shaping early Christian intellectual responses to the pagan revival under Emperor Julian the Apostate. Born likely in the early 300s, he first established his reputation in Berytus (modern-day Beirut), a renowned center of legal and rhetorical education in Phoenicia, before relocating to Laodicea in Syria. His significance lies in his ambitious literary project, undertaken with his equally prominent son, Apollinaris of Laodicea, to transform biblical narratives into classical Greek literary forms, thereby providing Christian youth with an education comparable to, and competitive with, the traditional pagan curriculum.

Faced with Julian's edict of 362 CE, which prohibited Christians from teaching classical literature, Apollinaris the Elder and his son embarked on an extraordinary endeavor. They meticulously paraphrased the Pentateuch into Homeric hexameters, rewrote historical books into Greek tragedies, and rendered the Psalms into Pindaric odes, all while composing comedies in the style of Menander. This monumental undertaking sought to demonstrate that Christian scripture could be presented with the same literary sophistication and pedagogical value as the revered works of Homer, Plato, and Demosthenes, directly challenging the pagan monopoly on higher education and cultural authority. Their work was not merely translation but a profound act of cultural appropriation and re-creation, aimed at legitimizing Christian intellectual life within the Hellenistic framework.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Apollinaris the Elder's innovative project to recast biblical texts into classical Greek forms was a crucial response to Julian the Apostate's anti-Christian policies, profoundly influencing the development of Christian education and literature in Late Antiquity. His work helped ensure the continuity of classical literary forms within a Christian framework, shaping subsequent Byzantine intellectual traditions.
